stories.author: leumon
stories.title: Genie 4 is now available
stories.groq_label: Google releases Genie 4 adding real time world editing native audio and a new creation agent for Project Genie Ultra subscribers
stories.groq_explain:
The article announces that Genie 4 is now available as part of a refreshed Project Genie experience for Google AI Ultra subscribers. The rollout adds the newest world model, Genie 4, along with upgrades to Genie 3, a new Project Genie agent, and a community gallery where users can discover, explore, and remix interactive worlds.

Genie 4 is described as the most realistic and interactive world model released by Google DeepMind. It lets users modify their environments in real time by typing new prompts while navigating a world, allowing changes to weather, characters, or actions on the fly. The model also introduces native audio that adapts dynamically to the visual scene, providing ambient soundscapes and character dialogue that evolve as the user explores.

Genie 3 remains available for longer sessions and for generating panoramas. The updated Genie 3 now supports three‑minute generations instead of sixty seconds, the ability to chain multiple worlds together for extended journeys, grounding of new worlds from 360‑degree panorama images, and real‑time in‑world events triggered by natural‑language prompts.

The Project Genie agent expands creation beyond single prompts. Users can describe a vision in natural language and the agent coordinates Google’s multimodal models to produce initial visuals, a signature aesthetic, and custom background music. Gemini models can be integrated into the session to observe the screen, offer context‑aware suggestions, and automatically trigger events.

A new gallery showcases curated worlds and community creations. Examples include “Living Memory,” which turns personal photos into explorable spaces; “Dino Field Guide,” a prehistoric habitat built from 360‑degree panoramas; and “Rock Paper Scissors,” where Gemini acts as a real‑time referee. Collaborative projects such as “Villa Giallo,” a gothic manor mystery created with technologist Will (BLVCKL!GHT), and “The Life of Ants,” a colony exploration built with filmmaker Anand Gandhi, demonstrate the capabilities of Genie 4’s photorealism.

The article emphasizes responsible development. All generated video and audio are watermarked with SynthID, and inputs and outputs undergo safety screenings. Genie 3 and Genie 4 remain frontier research models, and Google is actively addressing challenges like camera latency, complex physical interactions, precise real‑time audio, and long‑term scene permanence. A link to a Genie 4 model research overview is provided for further details.

Eligibility is limited to Google AI Ultra subscribers, who can start using the new Project Genie experience immediately. Google AI Pro members may join a waitlist. The page also offers a newsletter signup for product updates and related news.

stories.author: aray07
stories.title: The Magic of Partial Evaluation
stories.groq_label: Partial evaluation precomputes known inputs at compile time, generating specialized code that eliminates unnecessary runtime computation.
stories.groq_explain:
The article is a personal essay about the elegance of partial evaluation, a technique that separates the parts of a program that can be computed at compile time from those that must wait until runtime. The author begins by describing a fascination with software ideas that are beautiful in themselves, even if they lack immediate practical use, and explains that programming languages are a particular obsession because they allow solving whole classes of problems by stepping back to the meta‑level.

Partial evaluation is introduced through simple JavaScript examples. The factorial function called with a constant argument is shown to be fully reducible to the constant product 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1, meaning a sufficiently clever compiler could compute the result at build time and emit only the final value. A second example with a recursive power function where the base comes from the command line demonstrates how the same idea can reduce a program to a form that contains only the dynamic pieces (the unknown base) while eliminating the recursion.

The “big idea” is that a partial evaluator executes whatever can be determined statically and leaves the rest untouched. The author illustrates this with a tiny arithmetic interpreter that evaluates expression trees. When all operands are known, the interpreter collapses the whole tree to a single number. When a leaf contains an unknown value (e.g., `Number(process.argv[2])`), the evaluator still simplifies the surrounding structure, ending with an expression that mixes the unknown value with the computed constant part.

The piece then moves to a more ambitious example: a Brainfuck interpreter written in JavaScript. The author starts showing the code that sets up the tape, jump‑table, and pointer handling, hinting that partial evaluation can be applied to such an interpreter to generate a specialized, faster version—effectively turning the interpreter into a compiler for the specific Brainfuck program.

The motivation for writing the article stems from James Long’s revival of Meta’s JavaScript partial evaluator called Prepack. The author notes that Prepack prioritized practicality over beauty, which prompted a personal effort to create a new library that emphasizes the aesthetic and educational aspects of partial evaluation rather than production use.

Overall, the article explains what partial evaluation is, demonstrates its mechanics with concrete JavaScript snippets, and argues that the technique reveals deep connections between interpreters and compilers. It matters because it shows how reasoning about static and dynamic parts of a program can lead to automatic generation of optimized code, providing insight into language design and the nature of computation. The content ends part‑way through the Brainfuck example, so the full implementation and further discussion are not present. However, the existing text makes clear the author’s enthusiasm for partial evaluation and its potential to turn interpreters into “free” compilers.

stories.author: mooreds
stories.title: Scottish HTTP Codes
stories.groq_label: A humorous list of Scottish‑styled reinterpretations of HTTP status codes
stories.groq_explain: The page titled “Scottish HTTP Codes” is a tongue‑in‑cheek list that pairs standard HTTP status numbers with colourful Scots‑language phrases, many of which contain profanity. Each numeric code is followed by a short, often vulgar, colloquial expression meant to convey the same idea as the official status message but in a distinctly Scottish dialect. For example, 100 is rendered as “AYE, HAUD ON,” 200 becomes “NAE BOTHER,” 301 is “AWAY OWER THERE,” 404 is expressed as “NAE FUCKIN HERE, PAL,” and 500 appears as “AH’VE FUCKED IT.” The list covers a range of common client‑error, redirection, and server‑error codes such as 301, 302, 304, 307, 308, 400 through 425, 429, 431, 451, 500 through 505, and even the less usual 418 (“AH’M A FUCKIN TEAPOT”). The content is purely humorous, providing a cultural remix of technical status codes rather than any functional specification. Its significance lies in its playful use of regional slang to humanise and satirise internet protocol language, illustrating how technical jargon can be reimagined for comedic effect.

stories.author: gmays
stories.title: Seven new models at scalable price-performance
stories.groq_label: MAI launches seven new AI models delivering high performance at dramatically lower cost
stories.groq_explain:
The page announces seven new artificial‑intelligence models released by Microsoft at its Ignite 2026 event, emphasizing an unprecedented balance of capability and cost. The overarching goal is to keep developers and enterprises at the cutting edge while controlling the rising expense of token usage, allowing continuous, 24‑hour agent operation for real engineering tasks.

The first model, MAI Cyber 2 Flash, is positioned as a cyber‑defense engine that delivers “frontier intelligence” at a fraction of previous costs. It builds on earlier MAI Cyber versions, now costing 86 percent less per output token than MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash, and is already responsible for roughly 40 percent of scans in the MDASH system.

MAI Code 2 is the primary coding model, delivering 98 percent of the quality of GPT‑6.1 Sol on common enterprise coding benchmarks while costing only 40 percent of the price. It also reaches 96 percent of Claude Opus 5.5’s performance for just 5 percent of the cost. A variant, MAI Code 2 Flash, targets high‑volume, routine tasks such as explanations and quick edits, matching GPT‑6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65 percent and 20 percent of their respective prices. Both models are integrated into GitHub Copilot and available in limited preview through Microsoft Foundry.

The image‑processing offering, MAI Image 2.7, claims the top spot on the Artificial Analysis image‑editing benchmark, outperforming GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) while costing only one‑fifth as much. In text‑to‑image generation it ranks fourth overall, and the Flash version provides high‑volume image generation at about ten dollars per thousand images.

MAI Realtime 1 is introduced as Microsoft’s first live speech‑to‑speech model, delivering natural, low‑latency conversations and beating GPT‑Realtime 2.1 on both external and Dynamics 365 benchmarks. Its pricing starts at one cent per audio minute, making it viable for enterprise‑scale deployments.

The transcription service, Dragon Copilot Transcribe, runs on MAI Transcribe 2, described as the fastest and most accurate multilingual transcription model. It now handles ten million patient‑doctor encounters each month, halving error rates in multilingual workflows and reaching roughly one‑third of U.S. physicians.

Decision 1.1 is highlighted as a decision‑routing model that directs requests to larger, more expensive models only when necessary. It is claimed to be 50 times faster and 79 times cheaper than GPT‑6.1 Sol, and it leads the AA Decision Index ahead of competitors such as Jev, Google, and OpenAI. Approximately 4,000 customers are already using it.

In addition to the models, Microsoft announces the second‑generation AI accelerator, Maia 200, now in production and delivering 1.7 times more tokens per watt than previous hardware.

The announcement also underscores a push toward customizable models. Microsoft cites an example where AT&T built a custom MAI model for 5G network analytics that outperformed GPT‑6.1 Sol at fifty times lower cost, while noting that MAI Code 2 performed well in complex scenarios.

Overall, the release signals Microsoft’s strategy to provide high‑performance AI services at dramatically reduced prices, targeting continuous agent operation, enterprise coding assistance, image editing, real‑time speech, transcription, and decision routing. By coupling these models with more efficient hardware, Microsoft aims to keep its AI ecosystem competitive and attractive to a broad range of commercial customers.

stories.author: Kozmik1
stories.title: KVM: x86: Unconditionally reset MMU context when emulating INIT (CVE-2026-99312)
stories.groq_label: KVM x86 now always resets the MMU context when emulating an INIT instruction to address CVE‑2026‑99312
stories.groq_explain: The page is a CVE record for CVE‑2026‑99312, titled “KVM: x86: Unconditionally reset MMU context when emulating INIT.” Because the page content could not be extracted, the detailed description is not available. From the title, the entry concerns a security issue in the Linux Kernel Virtual Machine (KVM) for x86 processors. The vulnerability involves the handling of the INIT CPU instruction; when KVM emulates this instruction, it fails to properly reset the memory management unit (MMU) context. The fix requires that the MMU context be unconditionally cleared whenever an INIT is emulated, preventing potential exploitation such as memory corruption, information leakage, or privilege escalation. The CVE identifier indicates it was cataloged in 2026, and the record likely provides reference information, severity rating, affected versions, and mitigation steps for system administrators and developers. This matters because improper MMU handling can compromise isolation between virtual machines, undermining the security guarantees of virtualization environments.

stories.author: Betelbuddy
stories.title: AI agents ask better questions than KPMG accountants in audit trial
stories.groq_label: AI agents asked deeper, more insightful audit questions than KPMG accountants, highlighting a potential transformation of audit practices
stories.groq_explain:
The article reports that KPMG UK conducted an experiment in which more than one hundred artificial‑intelligence agents examined the financial statements of an unnamed FTSE 250 company. The trial, called Project Exponential, placed the AI agents alongside a conventional audit team and gave them tasks that covered the whole audit workflow rather than isolated administrative duties. The agents collected data, performed analysis, drafted conclusions and observations, and suggested next steps, while also coordinating with each other and dividing responsibilities.

KPMG’s head of audit, Cath Burnet, said the AI agents in several cases probed financial issues more deeply than the human auditors and raised questions that the audit team had not considered. The experiment showed that AI can go beyond boosting productivity and may fundamentally alter how complex financial information is examined, interpreted and challenged. Human oversight remained essential; an auditor intervened when an AI agent mis‑matched regulatory requirements with the company’s documentation, highlighting both the capabilities and the limits of current AI systems in dealing with intricate regulatory frameworks.

The firm plans to extend the approach to up to twenty larger audits but acknowledges that the technology is not yet mature enough for widespread deployment. Data quality is a key obstacle, as many businesses lack the clean, structured information needed for AI agents to function effectively. The potential impact on the accountancy profession is significant. Traditional audits rely on large teams of junior staff performing repetitive tasks under senior supervision, whereas AI agents could automate much of data collection, analysis and documentation, allowing senior professionals to focus on complex judgments and exceptions. This could lead to faster audits, lower operating costs and the ability to analyse larger volumes of data, though it is unclear whether any cost savings will be passed on to clients.

Regulatory and professional concerns are also raised. The UK Financial Reporting Council has warned that AI use must not compromise auditor independence, integrity or professional scepticism, and there are worries about data security, over‑reliance on automated conclusions and the risk of AI generating inaccurate or fabricated information. Ultimately, the responsibility for the audit opinion remains with the human auditor. The KPMG trial does not prove that AI can replace accountants or deliver a statutory audit on its own, but it demonstrates that AI agents are beginning to challenge tasks once thought to require uniquely human expertise. The key question for the accounting profession is not whether AI will enter the audit process, but how much of the process will eventually be performed by machines and what role human accountants will play as that shift occurs.

stories.author: gyre007
stories.title: Inside Deutsche Bank
stories.groq_label: Leaked Deutsche Bank documents expose systemic compliance failures, risky client deals, and involvement in illicit financial activities.
stories.groq_explain:
Inside Deutsche Bank is a website that presents a major investigative leak of more than fifteen million internal documents from the global banking institution. The leak is described as exposing a culture that prioritizes profit over compliance, revealing systemic blind spots and flawed internal practices across the bank’s most sensitive functions, including anti‑financial‑crime efforts, sanctions monitoring, internal auditing and the decision‑making units that determine whether high‑risk clients are retained or dismissed.  

The site lists a series of stories drawn from the leaked files. One story describes how the bank hired a member of a Qatari royal family, blurring the lines between investor, client and counterparty. Another details Deutsche Bank’s role in facilitating at least twenty‑four transactions worth roughly €173 million for Jho Low, the central figure in a massive kleptocracy case that remains unresolved. Additional reports claim that the bank’s documents show involvement in financing weapons used in Gaza, linking the bank to the supply of arms to conflict zones in violation of its own policies.  

Further articles allege that Deutsche Bank acted as a gateway for large‑scale money‑laundering schemes tied to a Russian oligarch, processed payments for a Hungarian bank that helped move billions of euros for Russian money, and financed blacklisted Spanish companies under investigation for corruption. The leak also includes evidence that the bank protected Russian client profits despite looming sanctions, and that it connected Trump‑owned companies to laundering operations.  

Other notable revelations involve a Deutsche Bank executive commenting dismissively on the misconduct of André Esteves, the head of Brazil’s BTG Pactual, a report that the bank’s payments to Jeffrey Epstein total roughly $600 million—twice the previously known amount—and documents showing the bank helped a Saudi prince set up offshore structures to manage a multi‑hundred‑million‑dollar investment portfolio.  

Collectively, the material suggests that Deutsche Bank’s internal controls were insufficient to prevent or address illicit activities, that the institution was complicit in facilitating financial crimes, sanctions evasion and the financing of conflict‑related industries, and that it maintained relationships with politically exposed persons and controversial clients. The significance of these disclosures lies in their potential impact on regulatory scrutiny, legal accountability and public trust in one of the world’s leading banks, as well as in highlighting broader systemic risks within the global financial system.

stories.author: speedping
stories.title: Unauthenticated remote code execution in Nginx
stories.groq_label: Critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX (CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007) affect HTTP/2 enabled servers, allowing attackers to take control.
stories.groq_explain:
The article reports the discovery of two critical, unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in the NGINX web server, identified as CVE‑2026‑123633 and CVE‑2026‑123007. These flaws allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code on a server running NGINX, potentially stealing data, altering websites, or disrupting services. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled, and the integer underflow issue (CVE‑2026‑123007) exists in versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 released in 2015, while the use‑after‑free issue (CVE‑2026‑123633) has been present for nearly six years.

The research was conducted independently by several groups, including Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint, and the findings were reported to F5, the company that maintains NGINX. The article outlines a coordinated disclosure timeline that began on October 21 2026 with the report of the first vulnerability, followed by a patch release and public disclosure on November 18 2026. The vulnerabilities are rated Critical with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2, highlighting the severe risk they pose to the world’s most widely used open‑source web server, which powers over 225 million sites.

The article emphasizes that the flaws reside in NGINX itself, meaning that even applications with secure code can be compromised if they rely on an affected NGINX instance. It also notes that the vulnerabilities were discovered using AI‑enhanced tools, specifically Wiz Atlas together with Gemini 4 Carbon and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol, illustrating how advances in artificial intelligence are lowering the barrier to finding complex memory‑safety bugs. This shift suggests that more longstanding vulnerabilities may be uncovered more quickly, increasing pressure on security teams to patch and mitigate.

For mitigation, the authors advise organizations to identify any deployments running vulnerable versions of NGINX with HTTP/2 enabled and to apply the forthcoming security updates as soon as they are available. If immediate upgrading is not possible, temporarily disabling HTTP/2 is recommended. The broader implication is that the security community must adapt to faster discovery cycles, ensuring rapid response and patch deployment to protect the critical infrastructure that depends on NGINX.

stories.author: DeepLogin
stories.title: 'Human' Is Cambridge Dictionary's Word of the Year 2026
stories.groq_label: Cambridge Dictionary chooses human as the 2026 Word of the Year, highlighting AI driven debates on what it means to be human.
stories.groq_explain:
The Cambridge Dictionary announced that “human” is its Word of the Year for 2026, reflecting the intense global debate about what it means to be human as artificial intelligence blurs the line between people and machines. The dictionary defines the term as having the qualities, faults and feelings of people, in contrast to gods, animals or machines. The selection highlights a year in which many public figures have defended human roles and creativity in the age of AI. Bill Gates argued that certain jobs, such as caregiving, should remain reserved for humans and emphasized that the success of AI should be measured by its benefit to human lives. Geoffrey Hinton warned that AI is creating alien beings and expressed a personal preference for humans, while Pope Leo XIV warned of new forms of de‑humanisation and called for a duty to remain profoundly human. 

Artists and writers also voiced concerns. Actors Scarlett Johansson and Cate Blanchett, musicians Tayla Parx, LeAnn Rimes and Billie Eilish, and authors Jodi Picoult and Jonathan Franzen criticized machine‑generated replicas as an assault on human creativity, launching campaigns such as the Human Artistry Campaign and the Artist Rights Alliance. Author Andy Weir wondered if he might be among the last fully human writers. The Authors Guild introduced a “Human Authored” kitemark for books, backed by Dame Mary Beard and Malorie Blackman. In response to AI deepfakes, actor Matthew McConaughey trademarked clips of his voice, face and catchphrase, and Taylor Swift did the same for her voice and image.

Academic commentary reinforced the theme. Professor Rachel Adams of the University of Cambridge noted that AI revives age‑old questions about human identity and that the technology could either deepen inequality or help solve it. Dr Tom McClelland, a Cambridge philosopher of science, said that the choice of “human” captures a shifting understanding of humanity as people compare human and artificial minds, focusing on consciousness, creativity and compassion, and urged young people to recognize that AI’s future is not predetermined. Lexicographer Colin McIntosh explained that AI is reshaping language about humanity, creating a zeitgeist that made “human” the most resonant word of the year. The announcement underscores how AI is prompting widespread reflection on human identity, rights, creativity and societal values.

stories.author: ritzaco
stories.title: DNS resolvers are the wrong place to fight piracy
stories.groq_label: Forcing DNS resolvers to block piracy sites is an ineffective and harmful policy, exemplified by Quad9's withdrawal from France.
stories.groq_explain:
Quad9, the Swiss non‑profit that operates the free 9.9.9.9 DNS resolver, announced that it will stop answering DNS queries from France on 24 November 2026. The decision is not driven by costs or a lack of users; it is a response to a Paris court fine for refusing to block a list of pirate sports‑streaming domains on behalf of beIN Sports. With around twenty similar cases still pending, the organization concluded that leaving France is the only viable option.

A DNS resolver translates domain names such as example.com into IP addresses that computers can reach. While most users rely on the resolver provided by their internet service provider, public resolvers like Google’s 8.8.8.8, Cloudflare’s 1.1.1.1, Cisco’s OpenDNS and Quad9’s 9.9.9.9 are available for anyone to configure. Quad9 is distinctive because it is a non‑profit founded in 2017 by the Global Cyber Alliance, IBM and Packet Clearing House, and it relocated its legal seat to Zürich in 2021 to anchor its privacy commitments in Swiss law. Its primary service is security filtering: it refuses to resolve domains flagged by threat‑intelligence feeds as malware, phishing or botnet infrastructure. Quad9 reports over 670 million blocks per day across more than 230 resolver clusters in over 110 countries and keeps no records of its users.

The French legal basis for the blocking orders is Article L.333‑10 of the Code du sport, introduced by the 2021 law that created the regulator Arcom. The article allows a sports rights holder to petition the president of the Paris judicial court for “dynamic” blocking orders that cover identified infringing sites and any future mirrors notified through Arcom. The wording includes “any person able to help stop the infringement,” which brings DNS resolvers within scope. In July 2026 the French parliament amended the law (Law 2026‑725) to create an automated real‑time blocking system managed by Arcom, removing the requirement for prior approval of each block. Quad9 called this development “recklessly dangerous.”

A series of court orders illustrates how the scope of enforcement has expanded. In December 2023 Canal+ sued Cloudflare, Google and Cisco to force DNS blocking of football piracy sites. By mid‑2024 a Paris court ordered the three resolvers to block about 117 domains; Google complied while Cisco withdrew its OpenDNS service from France. Subsequent orders in late 2024 widened the blocking requirements for Google and Cloudflare. In December 2024 Canal+ secured orders against Quad9 and Vercara, forcing Quad9 to block the domains worldwide because it cannot geolocate users. A beIN Sports request against Google, Cloudflare and Quad9 was rejected in May 2025 for insufficient evidence, a case Quad9 did not defend due to limited resources. In March 2026 the Paris Court of Appeal upheld DNS blocking under L.333‑10 for the first time, and later that month issued simultaneous orders against 19 ISPs, Google, Cloudflare, Quad9 and VPN providers. Additional orders in mid‑2026 targeted ISPs, Google, Cloudflare, DNS4EU, Whalebone and other resolvers. On 21 October 2026 the court imposed a penalty of €1,000 per day on Quad9 for non‑compliance, prompting Quad9’s announcement that it would cease service to France.

The article notes that many French public and private networks—including the interministerial digital directorate DINUM, France Travail, the CEA, Institut Pasteur, RENATER, EDF, SNCF, AP‑HM hospitals, France Télévisions, Thales and Airbus’s Stormshield—currently rely on Quad9. Because Quad9 does not keep user logs, it cannot notify these organisations of its withdrawal, and users will experience an abrupt loss of DNS resolution without an explicit error message. The piece argues that forcing DNS resolvers to block copyrighted content undermines the core security purpose of the service, threatens internet stability, and sets a concerning precedent for other jurisdictions.

The article ends abruptly after mentioning that the 21 October judgment is short and worth reading, indicating that the provided content is incomplete. Nonetheless, the available text makes clear that the author views DNS resolvers as the wrong place to enforce anti‑piracy measures, and that the French legal framework forces services like Quad9 to choose between compliance with censorship orders and maintaining their security‑focused, privacy‑preserving mission.

stories.author: DeepLogin
stories.title: ID.me terms required for IRS sign-in
stories.groq_label: ID.me’s IRS sign‑in terms mandate arbitration for disputes and permit data use for marketing unless users opt out within 30 days
stories.groq_explain:
The page explains that taxpayers who access IRS online services through the private‑sector sign‑in provider ID.me do so under ID.me’s own Terms of Service. Those terms send most disputes to a neutral arbitrator rather than a judge or jury, unless the user opts out within thirty days of acceptance. ID.me’s Privacy Policy states that it may use personal information for marketing, may share data in a corporate transaction, and can create a “wallet” that stores identity and group affiliation details. Although the policy says information from government‑verified identity checks will not be used for marketing on the ID.me Shop site without consent, the policy also allows promotional use and affiliate earnings through that shop.

The IRS permits both ID.me and the government‑run Login.gov for sign‑in, and the Direct Pay service allows tax payments without any sign‑in. ID.me replaced the traditional login for TreasuryDirect on 28 October 2026, prompting senators Ron Wyden and Elizabeth Warren to question the continued reliance on a private provider instead of Login.gov. The IRS describes ID.me as a private sector sign‑in provider that offers a “level of assurance” based on recognized standards and does not charge users a fee.

Key provisions of ID.me’s terms include an opt‑out right for arbitration within thirty days, a waiver of jury trials and class actions, and a requirement that users reaffirm acceptance of the prevailing terms at least once every five years or risk credential suspension. The Credential Policy, published in July 2024, outlines how identity proofing is performed. Users accept the terms by clicking an “Accept Terms & Continue” button; continued use after changes is deemed acceptance unless the user stops using the service and closes the wallet.

The article notes that a taxpayer shared a screenshot of the updated terms while signing in to IRS.gov, and that the most recent version of the terms (Version 10.1.0, dated 13 November 2026) counts continued use after revision as acceptance. Earlier versions required similar acceptance language. Legal commentary cited from a Marketplace interview highlights concerns that ID.me can alter its terms despite promises not to sell data, leaving users with limited recourse.

Overall, the page details the contractual and privacy implications of using ID.me for IRS authentication, the arbitration and waiver provisions that limit users’ legal options, and the broader policy debate about reliance on a private sign‑in service for government tax functions. This matters because it informs taxpayers of the rights they waive and the data practices they consent to when choosing ID.me as their gateway to federal tax services.

stories.groq_label: Google's AI Overviews cut traffic to external sites by about 40% as they dominate search results.
stories.groq_explain:
The article reports on a rapid rise in Google’s AI‑generated “Overviews” – concise, AI‑written summaries that appear above the traditional organic results – and the resulting decline in traffic to external websites. A randomized experiment that hid these Overviews from a subset of U.S. desktop Chrome users showed that when the summaries are visible, clicks to outside sites drop by roughly forty percent. The study measured an average of 0.37 outbound clicks per search with the Overview versus 0.62 when the Overview was hidden, a 39.8 % reduction. Searches ending with no outbound click rose from 54 % to 73 %, while ad clicks remained unchanged, indicating that Google is protecting its own ad revenue.

The prevalence of Overviews has surged dramatically. DataForSEO’s panel of 20 million keywords shows the share of results featuring an Overview increasing from about six percent in September 2024 to over sixty percent in August 2026. At the same time, traditional featured snippets fell from roughly nine percent to less than one percent, and the “discussions and forums” block also declined sharply. Video results and local map listings have grown modestly, but the dominant change is the dominance of AI Overviews across most search intents and keyword volumes.

The impact is broad. Across more than two thousand websites, the click‑through rate (CTR) for the top organic result on desktop fell from 17.8 % in September 2025 to 7.4 % in August 2026 – a drop of fifty‑eight percent. Mobile CTR declined as well, though less dramatically. The loss is not confined to high‑volume or high‑price keywords; even low‑volume queries and a wide range of cost‑per‑click tiers show similar rates of Overview appearance. Industry sectors differ, with health and finance queries receiving Overviews nearly seventy percent of the time, while apparel, dining and real‑estate see lower rates.

The article introduces “GEO” – generative engine optimization – as the emerging practice of getting content cited in AI‑generated answers. GEO essentially adds two steps to traditional SEO: ensuring presence on third‑party sources that AI draws from, and crafting pages that are easy for the AI to quote. However, the authors find little evidence that GEO currently compensates for the traffic loss caused by Overviews.

Two independent studies reinforce the findings. Pew Research Center’s survey of 900 U.S. adults found AI summaries on roughly eighteen percent of searches in early 2025, aligning closely with DataForSEO’s figures for the same period. A separate preregistered experiment with 1,100 participants also reported higher publisher clicks when Overviews were removed.

The significance of these findings lies in the shifting landscape of search traffic. As AI Overviews become the default presentation for a majority of queries, organic rankings no longer guarantee the same level of visitor flow. Publishers and marketers must reconsider strategies that rely on traditional SEO, potentially adopting GEO techniques or other approaches to maintain visibility. The research also highlights a broader industry challenge: balancing the convenience of AI‑driven answers for users with the economic health of the web ecosystem that depends on traffic from search results.

stories.author: subset
stories.title: Quad9's withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine
stories.groq_label: Quad9 is withdrawing its public DNS resolver from France following court-ordered domain blocking, highlighting broader risks to global internet infrastructure.
stories.groq_explain:
The Swiss non-profit foundation Quad9 recently announced the withdrawal of its free public Domain Name System resolver service from France. This decision followed a French court ruling that imposed daily financial penalties on Quad9 for refusing to block website domains associated with copyright infringement. Facing a choice between crippling legal penalties or altering its service in a way that compromises user privacy and security, Quad9 chose to shut down its operations in the country.

This withdrawal poses significant risks to French internet users and critical infrastructure. Quad9's public resolver is used across France by individuals, government bodies, educational institutions, hospitals, and public utilities. Because Quad9 has no direct contact information for its users, it cannot notify them of the upcoming shutdown. Any individual or organization that fails to switch to a different DNS resolver before the service is removed will experience unexplained internet connectivity failures.

Quad9's exit is part of a broader trend involving public DNS providers facing legal pressures in Europe. Cisco previously withdrew its OpenDNS service from France, Portugal, and Belgium under similar legal demands, and a Belgian court recently issued an order threatening substantial penalties against Cloudflare, Google, and Cisco if they do not begin blocking websites through their public resolvers by early 2027. 

The article argues that forcing public DNS resolvers to block websites is fundamentally ineffective and sets a dangerous precedent for internet infrastructure. DNS resolvers act as directory services, translating human-readable website names into numerical internet addresses. Removing an address from a public resolver directory does not remove the infringing content from the host server, and users can easily bypass the restriction by switching to alternative resolvers. Requiring core infrastructure providers to perform content blocking undermines internet reliability, security, and privacy while failing to solve online piracy.

stories.author: werrett
stories.title: Java4Shell: RCE in OpenJDK when processing Base64
stories.groq_label: OpenJDK HotSpot’s Base64 intrinsic contains an out-of-bounds write that enables heap leaks and remote code execution
stories.groq_explain:
The article, titled “Java4Shell: RCE in OpenJDK when processing Base64,” describes a security vulnerability discovered in the Base64 decoder of OpenJDK HotSpot on x86‑64 platforms and explains how the flaw can be turned into remote code execution.  

The author explains that while auditing the OpenJDK runtime, a memory‑corruption bug was found in the intrinsic used for fast Base64 decoding. The JIT compiler (C2) generates native code that employs AVX‑512 instructions, specifically the evmovdqub (VMOVDQU8) instruction, which writes bytes according to a 64‑bit mask. The mask calculation mis‑handles padding characters (‘=’) and can underflow, producing a mask of all ones (‑1 u64). When this mask is used, the intrinsic writes a full 64‑byte block to memory even though the allocated output buffer is smaller.  

For an input of 65 bytes (64 regular Base64 characters followed by ‘=’) the runtime allocates a 50‑byte buffer but writes 64 bytes starting at offset 48, overwriting memory beyond the buffer. On OpenJDK 17 the threshold input changes to 129 characters because the code path is reached later, but the same out‑of‑bounds write occurs.  

The write consists of fully controlled bytes at the first two positions of the 64‑byte block, while the remaining bytes are mostly uncontrolled except for a fixed pattern (0x9a) in the final 16 bytes. The author shows that, despite the limited control, the corruption can be leveraged using a classic JavaScript‑engine technique that overwrites the length field of a Java object (a buffer). By corrupting the length, the attacker can cause the object to accept arbitrary data and thereby corrupt neighboring objects on the heap. Combining this with heap‑feng‑shui, the out‑of‑bounds write can be turned into a heap leak and ultimately into remote code execution.  

The article emphasizes why the bug matters: it is a constant‑value overwrite in a widely used library, it bypasses typical mitigations such as ASLR, and it can be triggered remotely through malformed Base64 data. The exploit demonstrates that even mature platforms like OpenJDK can contain critical low‑level bugs that allow attackers to gain full control of the JVM process. The discovery also serves as a reminder to audit JIT‑generated intrinsics and other performance‑critical code paths, as they may introduce subtle memory‑safety errors.

stories.author: ibobev
stories.title: Web Browser Engineering
stories.groq_label: A guide to building a complete web browser in Python, covering networking, rendering, scripting, and modern features
stories.groq_explain:
Web Browser Engineering is an online book written by Pavel Panchekha and Chris Harrelson that explains how web browsers function behind the scenes. Although web browsers are ubiquitous in daily life, their internal mechanics are often obscure. The book addresses this by guiding readers through building a basic but complete web browser from scratch, spanning networking to JavaScript execution, using only a couple thousand lines of Python.

The text outlines the structure of the book, which begins with an introduction covering the history of the web and fundamental browser concepts. It is then divided into four comprehensive sections that progressively construct browser functionality. 

The first section focuses on loading pages, explaining how to handle URLs, make HTTP requests, create desktop windows, draw graphics onto a canvas, and format text with proper line spacing and word wrapping. The second section deals with viewing documents, covering how to parse raw HTML into a document tree, lay out elements using block and inline rules, parse and apply CSS styles, and handle user interactions with links and browser interface controls.

The third section addresses running applications, showing how to send data back to servers through form submissions, run interactive scripts that modify the DOM in response to events, and handle web security and privacy issues such as cookies, user logins, cross-site scripting, and cross-site request forgery. The final section covers advanced features of modern browsers, including GPU-accelerated visual effects, event loops and rendering pipelines, accessibility trees, support for embedded images and iframes, and optimization techniques like computation reuse and invalidation.

This material matters because it breaks down an extraordinarily complex, essential modern technology into an approachable, step-by-step engineering project. By building every layer of a browser in simple Python code, the project helps software engineers and web developers deeply understand how code written for the web is requested, parsed, rendered, secured, and executed.

stories.author: petecooper
stories.title: jQuery 4.1.0
stories.groq_label: jQuery 4.1.0 release introduces Ajax responseURL support, core loop refactoring, CSS selector fixes, data size reductions, documentation updates, selector enhancements, serialization improvements, and expanded test coverage.
stories.groq_explain:
The page records the GitHub release of jQuery version 4.1.0. It lists a single commit to the main branch since the release, indicating that the release is immutable and only the title and notes may be changed. The notes are organized by area of the library and describe a range of changes that were made for this version.

In the Ajax section the responseURL field was added to the jqXHR object, an alternative completeCallback API for transports was introduced, and a new commercial support vendor, TuxCare, was added to the documentation. Core changes include a refactor of loops to avoid array‑bounds issues, removal of the getElementsByTagName and getElementsByClassName methods in favor of querySelectorAll, improvements to CSS handling, use of createElementNS for XML documents, and a reduction in the library’s byte size. Documentation updates fix a spelling error, add guidelines for machine‑generated contributions, update the NES HeroDevs link, and refresh the active version table and README for the 4.0 release.

Selector updates work around a Safari regular‑expression bug, fix a regex issue in unescapeSelector, decode invalid escape code points to the replacement character, tighten duplicate removal in jQuery.uniqueSort, make quick‑selection paths stricter, address a regular‑expression denial‑of‑service vulnerability in identifier matching, and standardize document comparisons. The Serialize module adds support for form‑associated custom elements.

The Tests section adds new expectations for Chrome dimensions, relaxes error reporting in the parseXML test, accepts both old and new semantics for :enabled and :disabled selectors, introduces tests for jQuery.text, adds unit tests for callback‑only animation signatures, re‑enables AJAX binary data tests in Internet Explorer, adds tests for ajaxPrefilter and ajaxTransport, includes tests for .data() on SVG elements, and expands coverage of the serialize module.

Overall, the release bundles functional enhancements, performance and size optimizations, compatibility fixes across browsers, security improvements, and expanded test coverage, signalling continued maintenance and evolution of the jQuery library.

stories.author: dxs
stories.title: 350 years ago, this man discovered that light has a finite speed
stories.groq_label: Ole Rømer's 1676 observations of Io's eclipses provided the first empirical proof that light travels at a finite speed.
stories.groq_explain:
The article recounts how the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer, working in Paris in the 1670s, provided the first observational proof that light travels at a finite speed. In September 1676 Rømer warned members of the Académie des Sciences that Io, one of Jupiter’s moons, would emerge from the planet’s shadow on 9 November about ten minutes later than expected. His prediction proved correct, demonstrating that the delay was caused by the extra distance light had to travel as Earth moved away from Jupiter, and the opposite effect when Earth moved toward the planet.

Rømer’s method relied on the regular eclipses of Io, which he treated as a precise celestial clock. By recording the times of Io’s disappearances and reappearances over many months, he noticed that the observed times shifted systematically with Earth’s orbital position. From the magnitude of the shifts he estimated that light needed roughly twenty‑two minutes to cross the diameter of Earth’s orbit. This gave a speed of about 225 000 km s⁻¹, roughly twenty‑five percent slower than the modern value of 300 000 km s⁻¹, but the crucial point was establishing that light was not instantaneous.

Although earlier thinkers such as Empedocles, Ibn al‑Haytham, al‑Biruni and Roger Bacon had speculated about a finite light speed, Rømer was the first to demonstrate it with empirical evidence. His findings were published in December 1676 in the Journal des sçavans. Acceptance was gradual; some, including his own observatory director, were skeptical, but prominent scientists such as Christiaan Huygens and later Isaac Newton endorsed his work. A decisive confirmation arrived about fifty years later with James Bradley’s discovery of stellar aberration, which independently verified that light has a measurable speed.

Rømer’s discovery had lasting consequences for astronomy. Knowing that light takes time to travel means that observations of distant objects are glimpses of the past, a principle essential for understanding the evolution of the universe. The article emphasizes that while Rømer’s numerical estimate was imprecise by today’s standards, his demonstration that the speed of light could be measured opened the way for subsequent refinements and for modern cosmology.

stories.author: yonasb
stories.title: Launch HN: StarSling (YC P25) – Self-improving CI for agent-volume repos
stories.groq_label: StarSling offers fast drop-in GitHub Actions runners paired with AI agents that automatically optimize continuous integration workflows.
stories.groq_explain:
StarSling is an AI-native continuous integration service designed for GitHub Actions repositories, specifically tailored to handle high volumes of code generated by AI coding agents. It serves as a drop-in replacement for standard Linux runners such as ubuntu-latest, allowing software teams to speed up their verification pipelines by simply changing one line in their workflow configuration files while keeping all existing scripts and actions intact.

The core argument behind StarSling is that AI agents now write code faster than traditional continuous integration pipelines can check it, making pipeline execution and code review the primary bottlenecks for fast-moving development teams. StarSling addresses this issue through a combination of upgraded hardware infrastructure and self-improving software optimization tools.

A central feature of the platform is its AI agent functionality. Rather than acting as static hardware, StarSling uses intelligent agents that continuously analyze job execution logs, machine telemetry, and workflow steps. These agents automatically open pull requests to improve repository configurations by optimizing dependency caching, parallelizing jobs, updating test sharding, removing dead steps, and fixing security vectors. The platform also offers open-source agent skills that inspect workflows locally and guide coding agents on how to optimize continuous integration setups.

From an infrastructure perspective, StarSling utilizes high-performance fifth-generation AMD EPYC processors and features Adaptive Compute technology, which automatically routes jobs to the fastest available sandboxes and dynamically boosts CPU and RAM during running steps at no additional charge. It also provides persistent mounted disks for caching large dependency stores and build outputs, drastically reducing set-up time compared to default caching actions.

The service provides cost savings alongside performance gains. It charges by the second with no one-minute minimums, does not bill for queue time, and offers baseline four-vCPU Linux instances at rates roughly one-third cheaper than standard GitHub-hosted runners. It also supports GPU-backed runners for specialized workloads.

StarSling matters because software development teams adopting AI tools generate code faster than legacy continuous integration infrastructure can handle. By combining faster hardware, dynamic resource allocation, and automated pull requests that continuously rewrite and optimize workflow files, StarSling cuts build times significantly, lowers developer wait times, and reduces infrastructure costs without requiring teams to migrate away from GitHub Actions.

stories.author: pier25
stories.title: Solid 2.0
stories.groq_label: Solid 2.0 adds async‑aware fine‑grained reactivity and integrated server functions to enable distributed, high‑performance UI development.
stories.groq_explain:
The article marks the release of Solid 2.0, ten years after the project’s inception. The author reflects on the five‑year journey from the first commit to version 1.0 and another five years of development that led to this new version. The core premise that fine‑grained reactivity—implemented with signals—provides a solid foundation for user‑interface construction remains unchanged, but signals have since become widespread, appearing in Angular, Svelte, Vue and even in a TC‑39 proposal. Solid now positions itself as a stable, performant alternative that other frameworks can follow.

A major addition in Solid 2.0 is the “async graph.” Because fine‑grained reactivity knows the shape of an application, that knowledge can be extended to asynchronous data. Computations may now return promises or async iterators, and downstream code automatically handles pending states, race conditions and speculative rollback without requiring manual refactoring. An example shows a component that fetches a user profile with a memo and displays a loading fallback while the async value resolves. Server functions, introduced earlier in SolidStart, have been integrated into the core, enabling both RPC‑style request/response and persistent Server‑Sent Events. The article demonstrates a live server function that streams stock prices and how a component can memoize the result.

The release also emphasizes “built to be written by agents.” As AI‑generated code becomes common, Solid 2.0 provides diagnostics that can detect reactive mistakes at runtime. The fine‑grained graph records exactly what values were read and what should update, allowing the framework to report strict‑read errors with file location and suggested fixes. These diagnostics extend to detecting waterfalls, poorly constructed effect loops and inefficient graph shapes, and they are combined with linting rules, Chrome performance tools and an updated Sentry plugin to give developers and AI agents clear guidance during development and in production.

Experimental syntax support is introduced through ReactiveScript and TSRX, aiming to improve authoring for AI agents via compilation. The author argues that Solid’s composability restores the original promise of React’s ecosystem, providing primitive building blocks rather than a monolithic meta‑framework. Unlike newer frameworks that bundle a single router or cache solution, Solid now supports any router and offers primitives such as server functions and single‑flight mutation caches. The old Solid meta‑framework has been retired, reinforcing the goal of a single, flexible framework that can serve all use cases.

Overall, Solid 2.0 extends the original signal‑based reactivity with asynchronous capabilities, robust AI‑focused diagnostics, and flexible composability, positioning it as a performant, future‑ready alternative to more popular UI libraries. This matters because it offers developers a way to build distributed, server‑driven applications with fine‑grained control while also providing tooling that can safely integrate AI‑generated code.

stories.author: gnufx
stories.title: Purism Launches Librem 5 v2, a RISC-V Phone to Empower People
stories.groq_label: Purism launched a crowdfunding campaign for its privacy-focused Librem 5 v2 smartphone powered by a RISC-V processor and PureOS.
stories.groq_explain:
Purism, a Social Purpose Corporation focused on privacy, security, and digital freedom, announced a crowdfunding campaign for its next-generation smartphone, the Librem 5 v2. Positioned as an alternative to Android and iOS, the smartphone is designed to put users in control of their digital lives without requiring mandatory accounts or services from major technology companies like Apple, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon, or AI platform providers.

The device is powered by an eight-core RISC-V processor and runs PureOS, a fully free and open-source operating system. The transition to the open RISC-V architecture is central to Purism's effort to create an auditable, independent mobile platform free from proprietary chip designs. Key features include physical hardware kill switches that mechanically disconnect the camera, microphone, and wireless communications, as well as a privacy-by-design framework that minimizes data collection. Developing the phone on the RISC-V architecture will require substantial ongoing engineering work focused on graphics, peripherals, power management, and application compatibility.

The crowdfunding campaign is currently active, with the standard phone-only option priced at 1,599 dollars. Purism also offers payment plans and phone-and-cellular-service bundles. The company anticipates delivering the devices approximately 14 to 15 months after the campaign concludes, though it cautions that rewards and schedules are not guaranteed due to active development.

The Librem 5 v2 builds on Purism's prior crowdfunding and development efforts with the original Librem 5. As a Social Purpose Corporation, Purism incorporates digital freedom into its corporate governance and relies on a self-authored Digital Bill of Rights, which asserts users' rights to protect personal data, verify software, change providers, and avoid unwanted tracking.

stories.author: notmine1337
stories.title: Phrack 73 Released
stories.groq_label: Phrack 73 issue features 23 main papers and eight additional articles covering exploitation, reverse engineering, machine learning, hardware, and related research.
stories.groq_explain:
Phrack issue 73 is a new edition of the long‑running underground security magazine, released on September 30, 2026. The introduction reflects on the previous year’s celebration of Phrack’s 40th anniversary, noting that a special printed version was distributed at numerous conferences such as Defcon 33, HOPE, WHY25 and many others around the world. That anniversary edition featured a capture‑the‑flag competition, puzzles, easter eggs, parties and talks, all aimed at encouraging readers to dive into technical research and contribute their own work.

The current issue is described as the third release managed by the new editorial staff and larger than its predecessor, containing twenty‑three primary papers and eight additional articles. The content spans a wide range of topics, including exploitation techniques, reverse engineering, machine‑learning security, hardware research and cultural history. Specific technical highlights mentioned are container escapes using the vDSO, use‑after‑free exploits, QNX user‑land shellcode, Linux kernel investigations, a Chromium renderer sandbox escape via Skia, analysis of Windows smart‑card architecture, static taint analysis in Binary Ninja, and security concerns surrounding autonomous underwater vehicles. The issue also explores backdoors in machine‑learning models and the broader question of trust in AI systems, and it documents the path from a Phrack CTF challenge to two WinFSP zero‑day vulnerabilities. Historical pieces recount the infamous SSH‑1 CRC32 flaw that appeared in a film, the era of blue‑boxing free phone calls, a hacker’s confession about attempting a Linux kernel backdoor in 2003, and an early example of botnets for hire. A profile of notable researcher Halvar Flake is included.

Looking ahead, the editors speculate that rapid advances in artificial intelligence will transform vulnerability research and red‑team operations, making human intuition and creativity even more valuable. They call on readers to experiment with the ideas presented, challenge conclusions, and submit new work for future issues, emphasizing that the human side of hacking remains essential for shaping technology and society.

The article ends with acknowledgments to the conferences, sponsors, donors, artists, reviewers and logistical volunteers who helped produce the issue, and a disclaimer stating that the information presented is believed to be truthful to the best of the editors’ and contributors’ abilities. This issue matters because it continues Phrack’s tradition of disseminating cutting‑edge security research, preserving the historical narrative of the hacking community, and fostering collaboration and innovation among practitioners.
